slopes-curves-s1.title: A delivery van's fuel use at different speeds

table.caption: Gallons of fuel used per 100 miles at each steady speed (invented data for practice)

items.q: What is the slope of a line?
options: The change in the horizontal value divided by the change in the vertical value
The vertical value at the point where the line starts
The change in the vertical value divided by the change in the horizontal value
The sum of the two values at any point on the line

why.correct: Slope is rise over run: vertical change on top, horizontal change on the bottom.
options: That is run over rise, the slope turned upside down.
The starting height says where the line is, not how steep it is.
Right: rise over run.
Adding the coordinates of a point does not measure steepness.

items.q: A straight line passes through (20, 8) and (60, 4). What is its slope?

why.correct: Rise: $4 - 8 = -4$. Run: $60 - 20 = 40$. Slope $= \frac{-4}{40} = -0.1$, negative because the line falls to the right.

mistakes.why: That is run over rise. Put the vertical change (4 - 8) on top and the horizontal change (60 - 20) on the bottom.
The size is right but the sign is not: the vertical value falls from 8 to 4 as the horizontal value rises, so the slope is negative.

items.q: A phone bill is \$30 for 2 gigabytes of data and \$50 for 6 gigabytes, on a straight line with gigabytes across and the bill up. By how many dollars does the bill rise for each extra gigabyte?

why.correct: Slope = rise over run $= \frac{50 - 30}{6 - 2} = \frac{20}{4} = 5$ dollars for each gigabyte.

mistakes.why: That divides one point's values. Slope uses the CHANGES between two points: (50 - 30) over (6 - 2).

items.q: What is the slope of a horizontal line?
options: A negative number
The height of the line

why.correct: Along a horizontal line the vertical value never changes, so the rise is 0 and 0 divided by any run is 0.
options: Right: no rise, so the slope is 0.
A slope of 1 rises one unit for each unit across.
A negative slope falls to the right; a horizontal line does not fall.
The height says where the line sits, not how steep it is.

items.q: Line P falls 3 units for every 1 unit across. Line Q falls 1 unit for every 3 units across. Which statement is correct?
options: Both slopes are negative, and Q is steeper
P has a positive slope and Q a negative one
They have the same slope because both fall
Both slopes are negative, and P is steeper

why.correct: P has a slope of -3 and Q a slope of about -0.33. Both fall, and the one with the larger size (3) is steeper.
options: Q falls only one unit for three across, so it is flatter.
Both lines fall to the right, so both slopes are negative.
Falling tells you the sign, not the size; -3 and -1/3 differ.
Right: -3 is steeper than -1/3.

items.q: Along a straight line that falls to the right, how does the slope change as you move from left to right?
options: It becomes more negative
It stays the same
It becomes positive halfway along
It moves closer to 0

why.correct: A straight line has one slope everywhere. Only a curve changes slope as you move along it.
options: A curve that gets steeper does that; a straight line does not.
Right: a straight line keeps one slope.
A straight line does not turn around, so its sign does not flip.
A curve that flattens out does that; a straight line does not.

items.q: At what speed does the van reach the minimum point of its fuel curve?
options: 20 miles per hour
50 miles per hour
70 miles per hour
40 miles per hour

why.correct: Fuel use falls to 3.4 gallons at 50 miles per hour, then rises again. The lowest value marks the minimum point.
options: At 20 miles per hour the van uses the most fuel in the table.
Right: 3.4 gallons is the lowest value.
At 70 miles per hour fuel use is rising again.
At 40 miles per hour fuel use is still falling.

items.q: With speed across and fuel used up, what is the sign of the curve's slope between 20 and 40 miles per hour?
options: Positive, because both numbers in each row are positive
Zero, because the van keeps a steady speed
Positive, because the speed rises
Negative, because fuel used falls as speed rises

why.correct: From 20 to 40 miles per hour, fuel used falls from 6.0 to 3.8 gallons. A fall as you move right is a negative slope.
options: The sign of a slope comes from the CHANGES, not from the values being positive.
Steady speed describes each row, not how fuel changes across rows.
The run is positive, but the rise is negative, so the slope is negative.
Right: the curve falls over that range.

items.q: What is the slope of the fuel curve from 50 to 70 miles per hour, in gallons for each extra mile per hour of speed?

why.correct: Rise $= 4.4 - 3.4 = 1.0$ gallons; run $= 70 - 50 = 20$ miles per hour. Slope $= \frac{1.0}{20} = 0.05$, positive because the curve is rising.

mistakes.why: That is run over rise. Divide the change in fuel (1.0) by the change in speed (20).

items.q: What does the table show about the slope of the fuel curve as speed rises from 20 to 70 miles per hour?
options: It is negative, reaches 0 near the minimum point, then turns positive
It is positive the whole way
It does not change from one speed to the next, as on a straight line
It is negative the whole way

why.correct: Fuel use falls until 50 miles per hour and rises after it: a U shape, whose slope goes from negative through 0 to positive.
options: Right: the U-shaped pattern.
Fuel use falls at first, so the slope starts out negative.
The changes between rows differ, so this is a curve, not a straight line.
Fuel use rises after 50 miles per hour, so the slope turns positive.

items.q: Place point X on the downward-sloping curve D at a larger quantity than the point where D meets the upward-sloping curve S.

why.correct: D slopes down, so moving right along it to a larger quantity takes you to a lower price: X goes down and to the right along D.

items.q: Place point Y on the upward-sloping curve S at a smaller quantity than the point where S meets D.

why.correct: S slopes up, so moving left along it to a smaller quantity takes you to a lower price: Y goes down and to the left along S.
